approaches.title: Pre-registered fabric-versus-principal-stress angle on open femoral micro-CT
approaches.method: On open micro-CT of loaded cancellous bone, compute the local fabric tensor (mean intercept length, via BoneJ anisotropy) in a grid of cubic volumes of interest (edge about 5 mm in human femoral heads, scaled to trabecular spacing in other species) and the local principal stress tensor from a homogenized finite-element model of the same bone under a stated physiological load case (hip contact force direction and magnitude from Bergmann et al. 2001 / OrthoLoad for human femur). The statistic is, per volume, the angle between the primary fabric eigenvector and the principal stress direction of largest absolute magnitude, folded to 0-90 degrees. Two nulls are fixed in advance: (a) randomized fabric with the same density field, for which an isotropic random axis has median angle 60 degrees (P(angle <= theta) = 1 - cos theta); (b) a load-independent growth-rule null in which fabric follows a geometric field of the bone alone (local direction of the shaft or neck axis, and the gradient of distance to the cortical shell). Load-case sensitivity is tested by sweeping the load direction over a cone of 60 degrees around the physiological direction and recording the direction that minimizes median angular error; alignment is credited to load only if the best direction lies inside the physiological range and the error rises away from it.
steps: Scout and register datasets: human proximal femora (Twente/VPHOP femur database, FEMHALS if a data-use agreement can be signed, the CC BY Figshare femur section), plus at least one non-human loaded site on MorphoSource (primate or ungulate femoral head, calcaneus or vertebra) with licence recorded.

Pre-register in test-data/claim-tests/thompson-growth-form/thompson1917-ch16-05/: VOI size, fabric method, FE material law (density-dependent isotropic modulus, so fabric does not enter the stress computation), load case, angular tolerance (median error <= 20 degrees), and the pass rule (median error below both nulls at p < 0.01 by permutation, in at least three sites from two species).
Segment with a fixed global threshold (Otsu per scan, recorded), compute MIL fabric per VOI with BoneJ, discard VOIs with degree of anisotropy below 1.1 where the primary axis is undefined.
Build voxel or tetrahedral homogenized FE meshes (FEniCSx), apply the load case, extract principal stresses per VOI.
Compute angular error distributions, the two nulls (1,000 permutations for the randomized null), and the load-direction sweep; report all three sites separately and pooled.

Stratify by local stress anisotropy (sigma1 - sigma3)/(|sigma1| + |sigma3|): the stress-alignment hypothesis predicts error falls as anisotropy rises; the growth-rule null predicts no such dependence.
approaches.decisive_result: Median fabric-to-stress angle at or below 20 degrees in at least three sites from two species, significantly below both the randomized-fabric null (median 60 degrees) and the geometric growth-rule null, with the best-fitting load direction inside the physiological cone and error decreasing with stress anisotropy.
approaches.failure_signature: Median angle not distinguishable from the growth-rule null, or the error minimum in the load sweep lying outside the physiological cone or being flat (load-case insensitive); or fewer than three usable loaded sites with licences after scouting, in which case the approach stalls rather than refutes.

approaches.title: Calibrate the growth-rule null and re-orientation by remodelling simulation
approaches.method: The problem asks whether alignment is stronger than a load-independent growth rule would produce, but the size of that null is unknown. Simulate trabecular architecture on 2D and coarse 3D voxel domains (a femoral-head section and a rectangular block) under three rule families: (1) a Huiskes-type remodelling rule driven by strain energy density sensed by osteocytes with spatial influence decay; (2) load-independent rules (reaction-diffusion Turing-type patterning of bone deposition, and growth along a fixed developmental field such as radial distance from an ossification centre); (3) mixed rules with a tunable load weight w from 0 to 1. For each run compute the same fabric-to-principal-stress angle statistic as approach 1. Then rotate the applied load by 13 and 20 degrees, matching the magnitudes used in the guineafowl and sheep experiments (Pontzer et al. 2006; Barak et al. 2011), continue the simulation, and record the fabric re-orientation angle and its time constant.
steps: Implement the remodelling loop in Python with a voxel FE solver (FEniCSx or a sparse linear-elastic voxel solver), verify against the published qualitative outcomes of Huiskes et al. 2000 (aligned struts under uniaxial load, re-alignment after load rotation).
Implement the load-independent rules and the mixed-rule family; fix seeds and record all parameters.
For each rule and 20 seeds, compute the distribution of fabric-to-stress angles and the stress-anisotropy dependence.
Apply load rotation and record re-orientation angle versus simulated time.
Publish a lookup table: expected median angle and anisotropy slope for w in {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}, to be used as the pre-registered growth-rule null in approach 1.
approaches.decisive_result: A table showing that the alignment statistic separates load-driven (w = 1) from load-independent (w = 0) rules by more than the seed-to-seed spread, with the minimum load weight that produces a median angle below 20 degrees, and predicted re-orientation magnitudes for the two experimental rotations.
approaches.failure_signature: If load-independent rules on the same geometry produce median angles within the seed spread of the load-driven rule, the alignment statistic cannot discriminate causes and approach 1 must be redesigned around re-orientation; if results change by more than 10 degrees with voxel resolution or VOI size, the simulation is not converged.

references.note: Huiskes et al. 2000, Effects of mechanical forces on maintenance and adaptation of form in trabecular bone
Carter, Fyhrie and Whalen 1987, Trabecular bone density and loading history: regulation of connective tissue biology by mechanical energy
Pontzer et al. 2006, Trabecular bone in the bird knee responds with high sensitivity to changes in load orientation
Barak et al. 2011, A Wolff in sheep's clothing

approaches.missing: No wet data needed; this calibrates nulls and does not by itself settle whether real bone is aligned.

approaches.title: Lean proof that shear-driven rotation makes principal directions the stable fabric
approaches.method: Formalize the mechanism in claim thompson1917-ch16-06. For a plane stress state with principal stresses sigma1 > sigma2 and principal angle theta_p, the shear traction on a strut at angle theta is tau(theta) = ((sigma1 - sigma2)/2) sin(2(theta - theta_p)). Compare two rotation rules, k > 0. Rule A (signed shear): d theta/dt = -k tau(theta). Rule B (descent on shear energy): d theta/dt = -k d(tau^2)/d theta, which is proportional to -sin(4(theta - theta_p)). Prove: (i) under both rules the principal directions theta_p + m pi/2 are equilibria; (ii) under rule A the linearization -k(sigma1 - sigma2) cos(2(theta - theta_p)) is negative at theta_p and positive at theta_p + pi/2, so only one principal family is stable and Thompson's two orthogonal families (ch16-05) cannot both arise from it; (iii) under rule B both principal directions are asymptotically stable, the diagonals theta_p + pi/4 are the only other (unstable) equilibria, and V = tau^2 is a Lyapunov function non-increasing along trajectories; (iv) if sigma1 = sigma2 every angle is an equilibrium, so alignment is undefined under equal principal stresses. Part (ii)-(iii) says which reading of 'displaced by shear' is consistent with crossing tension and compression families; part (iv) yields the data prediction used in approach 1 that alignment strength should rise with stress anisotropy.
steps: Extend ThompsonLaws/Mechanics.lean with the shear traction formula derived from the existing stressAction (rotation of the symmetric tensor), proving tau is zero exactly on principal directions.
Prove the equilibrium characterization and the sign of the derivative at each equilibrium for rules A and B using Real.sin and Real.cos lemmas in Mathlib.
Prove V = tau^2 is non-increasing along any differentiable solution of rule B (HasDerivAt plus chain rule).
Prove the degenerate case sigma1 = sigma2.
Write the report entry under lean/reports with no sorry and standard axioms only, and link it to thompson1917-ch16-06.
approaches.decisive_result: A compiled Lean module with no sorry proving the four statements, recorded as formalized for thompson1917-ch16-06 in the lean reports, including the result that only the shear-energy rule makes both orthogonal families stable.
approaches.failure_signature: Needing a sorry for the stability or Lyapunov step, or a statement weakened to the point that it only restates tau = 0 on principal axes (already implied by the existing ch16-05 theorem).

references.note: Carter, Fyhrie and Whalen 1987, mechanical-energy regulation of trabecular density

approaches.missing: A proof shows the rule implies alignment, not that bone follows the rule; it does not address causality in organisms.

approaches.title: Meta-analysis of load-reorientation experiments for the causal arm
approaches.method: The causal falsifier (failure to re-orient after altered loading) can be tested on published experiments without new animals. Extract every controlled in vivo experiment in which joint load orientation or magnitude was changed and trabecular orientation measured against a control limb or group (starting with Pontzer et al. 2006 and Barak et al. 2011, plus studies found by a pre-registered search string in Europe PMC). The effect size is the change in primary fabric orientation in degrees relative to control, with the imposed load rotation as moderator. Fit a random-effects meta-regression of observed re-orientation on imposed rotation; Wolff's law predicts a slope near 1 (fabric tracks load) and an intercept near 0. Include studies with null results and record risk of bias (blinding, sample size).
steps: Pre-register the search string, inclusion criteria (controlled design, quantitative fabric angle, stated load-change angle) and the model.
Search Europe PMC and screen with two independent agents; resolve disagreements by a third.
Extract angles, SDs and n with page-level provenance; contact-free only, so studies without dispersion are recorded but excluded from pooling.
Fit the random-effects meta-regression (metafor, REML) and report the slope with 95% CI, heterogeneity I^2, and an Egger test.
approaches.decisive_result: Pooled slope of fabric re-orientation on imposed load rotation with 95% CI excluding 0 (causal tracking) and its distance from 1 (complete tracking), from at least five independent experiments.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than five eligible experiments, or a CI including 0, which would leave the causal claim unsupported; if eligible studies overwhelmingly report positive results with small n and Egger asymmetry, the pooled estimate is not credible.

references.note: Pontzer et al. 2006, Trabecular bone in the bird knee responds with high sensitivity to changes in load orientation
Barak et al. 2011, A Wolff in sheep's clothing
Christen et al. 2014, Bone remodelling in humans is load-driven but not lazy

approaches.missing: The number of controlled re-orientation experiments with extractable angles and dispersion may be below five; no wet lab to add new ones.

approaches.title: Pre-registered meta-regression of toughness enhancement over a constituent-only bound
approaches.method: Build a provenanced table of at least 40 records across at least five families (nacre, bone by site, dentin, enamel, antler, crustacean cuticle, sponge spicule) from primary papers cited in the Wegst 2015, Launey and Ritchie 2009, Barthelat 2016 and Ritchie 2011 reviews. Fix the toughness metric first: crack-initiation toughness K_IC and, separately, the maximum crack-growth toughness from J-R curves converted to K_J = sqrt(J E'), because hierarchy acts mostly on extrinsic crack-growth toughening and pooling the two would blur the effect. The constituent-only null is an energy mixing law G_mix = phi G_mineral + (1 - phi) G_organic with E from the Voigt-Reuss average, K_mix = sqrt(E_mix G_mix). The enhancement metric is log(K / K_mix). Regress it on platelet or fibril aspect ratio, mineral volume fraction, interface compliance proxy (organic layer thickness over platelet thickness) and the number of hierarchical levels counted by a written rule (a level counts only if it has its own characteristic length differing by at least a factor 5 from adjacent levels and its own documented deformation mechanism), with family as random effect. Validate by leave-one-family-out prediction.
steps: Pre-register metric definitions, extraction rules, the level-counting rule, the model and the pass thresholds in test-data/claim-tests.
Extract records with page and table provenance; two independent agents per record, discrepancies adjudicated.
Compute K_mix from constituent values reported in the same paper where possible, else from a fixed reference table of mineral and collagen/chitin properties stated in advance.
Fit mixed models: null (intercept only, i.e. constituents explain toughness up to a constant), architecture model, levels model; compare by leave-one-family-out RMSE.
Test monotonicity of enhancement in levels with an isotonic regression versus a flat model, controlling for volume fraction.
approaches.decisive_result: Leave-one-family-out RMSE of the architecture model at least 25% lower than the constituent-only null on log enhancement, and the level coefficient positive with 95% CI excluding 0 after controlling for volume fraction (compounding supported), or not (compounding refuted).
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than five families with both toughness and descriptors from comparable test methods; level counts that change under reasonable alternative counting rules (sensitivity analysis flips the sign); or measurement method (specimen size, hydration) explaining more variance than any structural descriptor.

references.note: Launey and Ritchie 2009, On the fracture toughness of advanced materials
Wegst et al. 2015, Bioinspired structural materials
Ritchie 2011, The conflicts between strength and toughness
Barthelat et al. 2016, Structure and mechanics of interfaces in biological materials
Fratzl and Weinkamer 2007, Nature's hierarchical materials
Wegst and Ashby 2004, The mechanical efficiency of natural materials

approaches.missing: Interface compliance and constituent toughness are rarely measured in the same study as composite toughness; hydration state and test geometry differ between papers and cannot be harmonized without new measurements.

approaches.title: Simulated fracture of self-similar staggered composites with 1 to 4 levels
approaches.method: Settle the compounding question in a model where constituents are held exactly fixed, which no dataset allows. Build 2D lattice-spring (or discrete-element beam) fracture models of the tension-shear staggered architecture (Ji and Gao 2004; Gao et al. 2003): level 1 is mineral platelets in a soft matrix; level n replaces each platelet of level n-1 with a scaled-up copy of the level n-1 composite, keeping the total mineral fraction fixed. Mineral and matrix springs have fixed stiffness and brittle failure strains. Load notched specimens in mode I to compute work of fracture and the resistance curve. Vary aspect ratio and mineral fraction at each level; compare against a single-level composite with the same total mineral fraction and against a random (non-staggered) arrangement of the same phases.
steps: Implement a 2D quasi-static lattice-spring fracture code (Python with sparse solvers), validated on the analytic tension-shear chain stiffness formula for level 1.
Generate hierarchical geometries for n = 1..4 at fixed total phi, with 20 random realizations each (platelet offset jitter).
Run notched fracture tests; record peak load, work of fracture, R-curve slope; check mesh and specimen-size convergence (specimen at least 10 times the largest level length).
Fit enhancement versus n and test monotonicity and saturation (isotonic versus logistic-saturation fit).
Write the predicted enhancement-per-level curve as the quantitative prior for approach 1's levels coefficient.
approaches.decisive_result: Curve of work-of-fracture enhancement versus number of levels at fixed constituents with realization-level 95% CIs, showing whether enhancement is monotone, saturating or non-monotone, and its sensitivity to aspect ratio.
approaches.failure_signature: Results that change by more than the realization spread when specimen size or lattice resolution changes (size effect not controlled), making the levels comparison an artefact; or failure to reproduce the level-1 analytic stiffness within 5%.

references.note: Ji and Gao 2004, Mechanical properties of nanostructure of biological materials
Gao et al. 2003, Materials become insensitive to flaws at nanoscale: lessons from nature
Lakes 1993, Materials with structural hierarchy
Barthelat et al. 2007, On the mechanics of mother-of-pearl

approaches.missing: A 2D spring model omits 3D crack deflection and twisting and fibril-level plasticity; it answers the compounding question for the model, not for real tissues.

approaches.title: Lean bounds: hierarchy cannot raise stiffness past the Voigt bound
approaches.method: Separate what hierarchy can and cannot do. Formalize the tension-shear chain effective modulus 1/E = 4(1 - phi)/(G_p phi^2 rho^2) + 1/(phi E_m) (Gao et al. 2003, with rho the aspect ratio, G_p the matrix shear modulus and E_m the mineral modulus) and prove: (i) E is increasing in rho and bounded above by phi E_m; (ii) applying the formula recursively, with level n using the level n-1 modulus as its 'mineral', the modulus at every level is bounded by the Voigt bound of the total mineral fraction, so stiffness cannot compound with levels; (iii) the strength of the level-n composite is bounded by the mineral strength times the total volume fraction under the same chain model. The result sharpens the problem: any compounding must be in toughness (energy dissipation), which is where the data test and the simulation should look, and claims of compounding stiffness or strength are refuted by the model itself.
steps: Write ThompsonLaws/Biocomposite.lean defining the chain modulus and the recursive hierarchy.
Prove monotonicity in rho and the upper bound phi E_m (field_simp, positivity, div_le_iff).
Prove the recursive bound by induction on the level, with total fraction the product of per-level fractions.
Prove the strength bound under the stated load-transfer assumptions.
Record in lean/reports and link to thompson1917-ch16-02 as a supporting formal statement, not as a proof of the claim.
approaches.decisive_result: Compiled Lean module with no sorry stating the stiffness and strength bounds for arbitrary numbers of levels.
approaches.failure_signature: The recursive bound requires assumptions (e.g. matrix shear modulus scaling across levels) that cannot be stated without making the theorem vacuous.

references.note: Gao et al. 2003, Materials become insensitive to flaws at nanoscale: lessons from nature
Ji and Gao 2004, Mechanical properties of nanostructure of biological materials

approaches.title: Formalize the constrained optimum: empty tubes have none, filled tubes do
approaches.method: The question presupposes an interior stiffness-per-mass optimum, but for an empty thin-walled tube at fixed mass (fixed r t) the bending stiffness E pi r^3 t grows as r^2, so stiffness per mass increases without bound as K = r_inner/r_outer goes to 1 and only local buckling (Brazier ovalisation, whose collapse moment scales as E r t^2 / sqrt(1 - nu^2)) or another constraint stops it. With a marrow or pith core of density ratio q = rho_core/rho_wall that must be carried, Currey and Alexander (1985) showed an interior optimum K*(q) exists. Formalize: (i) for an empty tube, stiffness-per-mass at fixed outer radius is strictly increasing in K on [0, 1); (ii) with core mass included, the mass at fixed bending stiffness has a unique minimum K*(q) in (0, 1) for q in (0, 1), and K* decreases as q increases; (iii) under a Brazier constraint the feasible set is K <= K_b(E, sigma_allow), so the predicted K is min(K*(q), K_b). These three lemmas turn the vague 'optimum' into three numerical predictions per structure: pneumatic (q = 0) structures should sit at the buckling limit, filled structures at K*(q).
steps: Define I(K) = (pi/4) R^4 (1 - K^4), wall area pi R^2 (1 - K^2), core area pi R^2 K^2 in Lean.
Prove the empty-tube monotonicity lemma.

Prove existence and uniqueness of the minimum-mass K* at fixed stiffness for core density ratio q in (0,1), via the derivative sign or an explicit convexity argument after the substitution x = K^2, and the monotone dependence on q.
State the Brazier feasibility constraint as a hypothesis-parameterized inequality and prove the min rule.
Compute K*(q) numerically for q in the range of marrow (fatty and haematopoietic) and pith densities, and store the table for approach 2.
approaches.decisive_result: Compiled Lean module with no sorry proving the three lemmas, plus a numeric K*(q) table that makes the data test's predictions explicit.
approaches.failure_signature: Uniqueness of K* cannot be proved without restricting q to a narrower interval than real marrow and pith densities span, in which case the prediction is not well defined for some structures.

references.note: Currey and Alexander 1985, The thickness of the walls of tubular bones
Gibson, Ashby, Wegst and Olive 1995, The mechanical properties of natural materials II

approaches.title: Cross-taxon test of K against marrow-adjusted optimum and buckling limit
approaches.method: Compile at least 100 structures from four types: marrow-filled mammal long bones, pneumatic and marrow-filled bird long bones, bamboo culms and hollow grass stems, and feather rachises, each with outer radius, wall thickness and tissue modulus from the same or a matched source. For each, compute three predictions from approach 1: K*(q) (core-mass-adjusted stiffness optimum), K_b (Brazier local-buckling limit using measured E and an assumed strength-to-modulus ratio stated per tissue) and the predicted value min(K*, K_b). The sharpest test is within birds: pneumatic bones carry no marrow mass, so they are predicted to sit nearer K_b, while marrow-filled bones of the same birds should sit near K*(q). Classify each structure as at-optimum (|K - K*| <= 0.05), at-buckling (|K - K_b| <= 0.05), or neither; test size dependence by regressing K on log body or structure mass with phylogenetic GLS for the animal subset.
steps: Pre-register the tolerance (0.05 in K), the q values per tissue, and the classification rule.
Extract K and E from Currey and Alexander 1985 and other primary tables found by a pre-registered search; resolve taxa through the organisms layer (GBIF, NCBI).
Compute predictions and classify; run the paired pneumatic-versus-marrow comparison with a sign test and a mixed model with species as random effect.
Fit K versus log mass, phylogenetically corrected for vertebrates.
approaches.decisive_result: Proportions of structures at K*, at K_b and at neither, with the pneumatic-versus-filled contrast in birds; Thompson's optimality claim is supported if most filled structures fall within 0.05 of K* and pneumatic ones are shifted toward K_b.
approaches.failure_signature: Most structures fall in the 'neither' class, or the pneumatic-filled contrast is absent or reversed; or fewer than 100 structures have a matched modulus, in which case the test is underpowered rather than decisive.

references.note: Currey and Alexander 1985, The thickness of the walls of tubular bones
Ashby, Gibson, Wegst and Olive 1995, Material property charts
Gibson, Ashby, Wegst and Olive 1995, Microstructures for mechanical efficiency

approaches.missing: Matched tissue moduli for feather rachises and many plant stems are sparse; bird pneumaticity status per bone must be extracted from anatomical literature.

approaches.title: Measure K along the shaft from open CT and test the bending-moment profile
approaches.method: Use open CT of limb bones (MorphoSource, with licences recorded) to measure K and cortical thickness at 5% increments along the diaphysis in at least 60 bones across mammals and birds spanning three orders of magnitude in body mass. This gives both a size-dependent test of K at mid-shaft and a direct test of the companion claim thompson1917-ch16-04 (already formalized in Lean as uniformStressThickness_max_mid): wall thickness should track the bending-moment profile of a stated load case. Segment cortical bone with a fixed threshold, compute second moments of area and K per slice, and regress the thickness profile on the bending-moment profile of a three-point-bending load case with the actual bone length.
steps: Scout MorphoSource for open-download femora and humeri with voxel size below 1% of shaft diameter; record licences.
Pre-register slice spacing, threshold rule, load case and the pass criterion (Pearson r >= 0.7 between thickness and moment profiles in most bones; mid-shaft K within 0.05 of K*(q) from approach 1).
Run segmentation and cross-section geometry (BoneJ slice geometry).
Fit K versus log body mass with phylogenetic GLS; report the thickness-moment correlation per bone.
approaches.decisive_result: Distribution of mid-shaft K versus body mass and of the thickness-to-moment correlation across at least 60 bones, against the pre-registered thresholds.
approaches.failure_signature: Thickness profiles that peak away from mid-shaft in most bones (e.g. near muscle insertions), or too few open-download specimens to span the mass range.

approaches.title: Pre-registered PGLS of circumference on mass with three fixed exponents
approaches.method: Translate the hypotheses to circumference C (the measure Campione and Evans use): geometric similarity predicts C proportional to M^(1/3), elastic similarity M^(3/8), stress similarity with constant posture M^(1/2) (area proportional to M). Combine the Campione and Evans 2012 supplementary data with an independent compilation (e.g. Alexander et al. 1979 and further published tables found by a pre-registered search) to reach at least 300 quadrupedal taxa, resolve names through the organisms layer and match to a time-calibrated phylogeny (Upham et al. 2019 for mammals; a published composite tree for reptiles and amniotes stated in advance). Fit PGLS with Pagel's lambda estimated by ML (phylolm), separately for humerus, femur and combined circumference, and report both OLS-type and standardized major axis slopes, because the choice changes the exponent and is a known source of disagreement. A hypothesis is accepted if its exponent lies inside the 95% CI and the CI half-width is at most 0.02; the three values differ by 0.042 and 0.125, so the tolerance must be tighter than half the smallest gap.
steps: Download Campione and Evans 2012 additional files; record the exact file and checksum.
Pre-register hypotheses, regression type, tree source, lambda handling, tolerance 0.02 and the clade partition.
Assemble the independent compilation and run a pre-specified duplicate check against Campione and Evans taxa.
Fit PGLS globally and per bone; bootstrap over 100 posterior trees to propagate tree uncertainty.
Report which hypotheses lie in each CI; also refit on the independent compilation alone as a replication.
approaches.decisive_result: Global phylogenetic exponent of C on M with 95% CI of half-width at most 0.02, stating which of 1/3, 3/8, 1/2 it includes, replicated on the independent compilation.
approaches.failure_signature: CI too wide to separate 1/3 from 3/8 (fewer usable taxa than expected), or the exponent differing between the two compilations by more than the CI, indicating measurement or mass-estimation inconsistency.

approaches.title: Clade and posture heterogeneity of exponents by phylogenetic ANCOVA
approaches.method: The falsifier is clade-dependent exponents. On the dataset of approach 1, fit phylogenetic ANCOVA models with clade-specific slopes (Mammalia orders with at least 15 species, squamates, testudines, crocodylians) and a posture covariate coded in advance (sprawling, semi-erect, erect; cursorial versus not), and compare a single-slope model against clade-slope and posture-slope models by AICc and likelihood ratio, with tree uncertainty propagated over posterior trees. Biewener's posture hypothesis predicts that once posture is in the model, residual clade slopes are not needed; a single mechanical law predicts the single-slope model wins outright.
steps: Pre-register clade partition, posture coding (from literature, coded blind to bone data), minimum clade size and model set.
Fit single, clade-slope, posture-slope and clade-plus-posture models (phylolm, or MCMCglmm with tree as random effect).
Report per-clade exponents with CIs against the three hypotheses.
Check robustness to removing the largest-bodied taxa (elephants, rhinoceroses) and to SMA versus OLS.
approaches.decisive_result: Delta AICc and LR test of the single-slope model versus clade-slope and posture-slope models, with per-clade exponent CIs.
approaches.failure_signature: Clade sample sizes too small to estimate slopes with CI half-width below 0.05, making heterogeneity undetectable rather than absent.

references.note: Biewener 1989, Scaling body support in mammals: limb posture and muscle mechanics
Campione and Evans 2012

approaches.title: Lean derivation of similarity exponents and the posture-compensation identity
approaches.method: Formalize the three hypotheses as power-law assumptions and derive the exponents, extending Magnitude.lean (which already proves the strength/weight argument for thompson1917-ch02-03). Geometric similarity: all lengths proportional to M^(1/3), so area M^(2/3). Elastic similarity (McMahon): diameter d proportional to l^(3/2) and M proportional to l d^2, so d proportional to M^(3/8), area M^(3/4), length M^(1/4). Stress similarity with posture: peak bone stress sigma proportional to M / (A times EMA) up to a bone-geometry factor; if A proportional to M^a and EMA proportional to M^e then sigma proportional to M^(1 - a - e), so constant stress (flat safety factor if strength is size-independent) requires a + e = 1. Prove these as theorems over real exponents. Then plug in the published estimates of a (from approach 1) and of e (Biewener 1989) to state the implied stress exponent with propagated uncertainty, giving a numerical test of whether the safety factor is flat.
steps: Define power-law scaling relations as functions f(M) = c M^p with Real.rpow and prove the composition lemmas.
Prove the three exponent derivations and the stress identity sigma exponent = 1 - a - e.
Prove that a + e = 1 is necessary and sufficient for size-independent stress under the stated model.
Record in lean/reports; compute 1 - a - e with delta-method or bootstrap CIs using approach 1's a and Biewener's e, labelled as a data-dependent corollary, not a theorem.
approaches.decisive_result: Compiled Lean module with no sorry for the derivations and the identity, plus the stress-exponent estimate with 95% CI and whether it includes 0.
approaches.failure_signature: The data step: if EMA estimates exist for too few species to give a CI on e narrower than 0.1, the safety-factor question stays open even though the formal part completes.

references.note: McMahon 1973, Size and shape in biology
Biewener 1989, Scaling body support in mammals

approaches.missing: Effective mechanical advantage data across many species are limited to a few published compilations.

approaches.title: Literature-extracted test of curvature and h^2/D response time across species
approaches.method: Extend the repo's pre-registered pine-cone curvature test to the full acceptance criterion using published data only. For each specimen or specimen class in pine cone scales (Reyssat and Mahadevan 2009; Quan et al. 2021; Eger et al. 2022; Dawson et al. 1997), wheat awns (Elbaum et al. 2007), chiral seed pods (Armon et al. 2011) and fabricated bilayers (paper-polymer in Reyssat and Mahadevan; Erb et al. 2013; Gladman et al. 2016; Le Duigou and Castro 2016), extract layer thicknesses, moduli, free swelling strains, diffusivity or permeability, measured curvature change and response time. Predict curvature with the Lean-checked Timoshenko formula (bilayerCurvature_ofEquilibrium) and response time with tau = h^2/D (diffusiveTime_scale). Pass: |log(kappa_measured/kappa_pred)| <= log 1.5 in most specimens; response time slope on log h equals 2 within plus or minus 0.4 among fabricated bilayers of at least three thicknesses.
steps: Pre-register tolerances, extraction rules (only inputs measured independently of the curvature itself; no back-fitted swelling strains) and the specimen count required (20 specimens, five species, or the fabricated-bilayer alternative).
Extract from text, tables and digitized figures (with digitization error recorded).
Compute predictions and residuals; report per species.
Fit log tau on log h for fabricated series with a mixed model by study; report slope and CI.
Classify deviations by suspected cause (fibre angle, gradient, viscoelasticity) for approach 2.
approaches.decisive_result: Per-specimen curvature ratio distribution and response-time exponent with CI, against the pre-registered tolerances.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than 20 specimens with all inputs independently measured (most papers fit swelling strain from curvature, which is circular); response time series with fewer than three thicknesses.

approaches.title: FE correction factors for fibre angle, gradients and poroelastic lag
approaches.method: Quantify, before looking at data, how far real hygromorph features push curvature and response time from the Timoshenko and h^2/D predictions. Run FEniCSx models of strips with (a) misaligned swelling direction at angle phi (reducing bending and adding twist, consistent with the Lean-checked antisymmetric-twist theorems), (b) continuously graded modulus and eigenstrain through the thickness, (c) imperfect bonding via a compliant interlayer, (d) poroelastic coupling with layer-specific diffusivities, and (e) linear viscoelastic relaxation. Produce dimensionless correction maps kappa_FE/kappa_Timoshenko and tau_FE/(h^2/D) over the parameter ranges reported for pine cones, awns and printed bilayers. These maps convert approach 1 from a pass/fail of the ideal model into a test of whether measured deviations are explained by measured structure.
steps: Verify the FE code against the Timoshenko formula (error below 1% for slender, perfectly bonded, uniform layers) and against the first diffusion mode decay rate pi^2 D/h^2.
Sweep each departure separately over literature ranges, then in pairs.
Publish correction tables and the parameter region where Timoshenko is within 10%.
Pre-register their use as the 'structure-corrected' model in approach 1.
approaches.decisive_result: Correction maps with the boundary of the 10% validity region of the ideal model for each departure, checked for mesh convergence.
approaches.failure_signature: Corrections that depend on unmeasured parameters (e.g. interlayer compliance) so strongly that any measured curvature can be fitted, making the corrected model unfalsifiable.

references.note: Timoshenko 1925, Analysis of bi-metal thermostats
Armon et al. 2011, chiral seed pods

approaches.title: Lean: graded-beam curvature integral reducing to Timoshenko
approaches.method: Generalize the existing Hygromorphs.lean results from two uniform layers to arbitrary through-thickness profiles E(z) and eigenstrain eps(z). With moments A = integral E, B = integral E z, D = integral E z^2, P = integral E eps, Q = integral E z eps over the thickness, force and moment balance give curvature kappa = (A Q - B P)/(A D - B^2). Prove this from equilibrium for integrable profiles (interval integrals in Mathlib), prove A D - B^2 > 0 for positive non-constant-free E (Cauchy-Schwarz), and prove it reduces to the existing bilayerCurvature for piecewise-constant two-layer profiles. Also prove that for a two-layer strip with diffusivities D1 and D2 the slowest diffusion time lies between h^2/(pi^2 D_max) and h^2/(pi^2 D_min) for the stated separable model, or state the bound as a conditional theorem if the spectral argument exceeds current Mathlib.
steps: Define the moment integrals with intervalIntegral and state equilibrium.
Prove the curvature formula and the positivity of the denominator.
Prove the reduction to bilayerCurvature for two-layer step profiles.
Attempt the diffusion-time bracket; if not feasible, record precisely what Mathlib lacks.
Update the Hygromorphs report.
approaches.decisive_result: Compiled Lean theorems for the graded curvature formula and its reduction to Timoshenko, with no sorry.
approaches.failure_signature: Integration lemmas for piecewise-constant functions too cumbersome to close the reduction; diffusion bracket left unproved (partial completion).

references.note: Timoshenko 1925, Analysis of bi-metal thermostats

approaches.missing: The diffusion-time bracket for heterogeneous layers needs spectral theory of Sturm-Liouville operators that Mathlib may not provide.

approaches.title: Mesh statistics of radiolarian lattice shells against foam and two Voronoi nulls
approaches.method: Reuse the cell-geometry pipeline (Cellpose segmentation, junction-angle and neighbour-count analysis, synthetic controls) on images of latticed radiolarian shells. Primary data must be micrographs (SEM or light), because Haeckel's plates are idealized drawings; use them only as a secondary, explicitly flagged set. Measure in the central region of each shell where foreshortening is below 10% (or correct projection on a fitted sphere): fraction of trivalent vertices, vertex-angle SD around 120 degrees, polygon-side distribution and its second moment mu2, Lewis's law slope (pore area versus sides) and Aboav-Weaire. Compare to three references fixed in advance: a relaxed foam (Plateau borders, simulated by vertex model at matched polydispersity), a Poisson-Voronoi null, and a hard-core (equal-sized random packing) Voronoi null. The hard-core null is essential: equal vesicle packing alone yields many hexagons without surface tension, so only vertex angles and mu2 at matched polydispersity can separate surface-tension moulding from packing. Euler's relation forces mean sides near 6 on any trivalent net, so mean side number is excluded as evidence (the lesson of the repo's ch07-10 result).
steps: Scout image sources with licences: mikrotax radiolaria pages, the Tetard et al. 2020 radiolarian image workflow data, Wikimedia Commons, and open-access SEM figures; record species, mineral and magnification.

Pre-register: at least 30 shells, the central-region rule, the metrics, the nulls, and the match criterion (vertex-angle SD and mu2 closer to the foam reference than to both Voronoi nulls, by bootstrap over shells).
Segment pores (Cellpose via Nebius, or classical watershed if Cellpose fails on lattice images; compare both).
Simulate the three references at each shell's measured pore-size polydispersity.
Report per shell and pooled; publish as a claim test on thompson1917-ch09-14.
approaches.decisive_result: For at least 30 micrograph-imaged shells, vertex-angle SD and mu2 significantly closer to the matched foam reference than to both Poisson and hard-core Voronoi nulls (or not), with segmentation error bounded by synthetic-lattice calibration.
approaches.failure_signature: Segmentation of 3D lattice shells in 2D images too unreliable (calibration error larger than the foam-versus-hard-core gap), or fewer than 30 licensed micrographs.

approaches.title: Equivalence test of lattice regularity across silica, SrSO4 and organic shells
approaches.method: Test the mineral-independence claim (thompson1917-ch09-15) directly: compare mesh-regularity metrics from approach 1 (vertex-angle SD, mu2, hexagon fraction at matched polydispersity) between silica lattice shells (Spumellaria), strontium sulphate lattice shells (Acantharia with latticed shells) and the organic lattice of Clathrulina. Use two one-sided tests (TOST) with an equivalence margin fixed in advance from a pilot on synthetic lattices (the margin is set to half the difference in each metric between the matched foam reference and the hard-core Voronoi null of approach 1, so 'equivalent' means closer than the physics-versus-packing distinction can resolve), with mixed models by taxon. Equivalence supports mineral-independent moulding; a mineral effect beyond the margin refutes it. The underlying vesicle pattern is not observable in fixed shells, so this tests mineral-independence of the final geometry, not 'given the same vesicle pattern'; that limitation is stated.
steps: Scout images for each mineral group, with at least 10 shells per group; Clathrulina SEM is the likely bottleneck.
Pre-register metrics, margin and the mixed-model TOST.
Run approach 1's pipeline on all shells.
Report equivalence or difference per metric.
approaches.decisive_result: TOST result per metric across the three mineral groups, with at least 10 shells each.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than 10 usable Clathrulina or latticed acantharian images, leaving the comparison underpowered.

references.note: Weiner and Addadi 2011, Crystallization pathways in biomineralization

approaches.missing: Open micrographs of Acantharia lattice shells and Clathrulina in sufficient number; no culture or microscope to generate them.

approaches.title: Spherical vesicle-foam simulation with Plateau-border deposition
approaches.method: Generate the physical prediction explicitly rather than borrowing planar foam statistics. Simulate a monolayer of N vesicles on a sphere with a 2D vertex model (line tension on edges, area constraint per vesicle, polydispersity parameter s), relax to equilibrium, and deposit mineral along edges (Plateau borders). Vary N and s. Record pore polygon distribution, vertex angles, defect (non-hexagon) positions and their spacing. Two physics checks that are not discriminating, and should be reported as such: on any trivalent spherical net the sum over faces of (6 - n) is exactly 12 (Euler), and mean sides approach 6 as N grows. The discriminating outputs are the vertex-angle distribution, the defect-correlation length (defects in relaxed foams arrange in scars or are spread; in random packings they are uncorrelated) and Lewis-law slope at a given s. Fit s per real shell and test whether a single s reproduces all statistics jointly (posterior predictive check).
steps: Implement a spherical vertex model in Python (or use Surface Evolver if available) and verify against known results for monodisperse 2D foams.
Prove or cite the Euler identity sum (6 - n) = 12 for trivalent spherical nets (a short Lean lemma assuming V - E + F = 2 and trivalence).
Sweep N in 20..500 and s in 0..0.5; build summary-statistic emulators.
Fit s per shell from approach 1 data by approximate Bayesian computation and run joint posterior predictive checks.
approaches.decisive_result: Posterior predictive p-values for the joint statistics of each shell under the fitted foam model; most shells reproduced (p > 0.05) supports the physical explanation, systematic failure in vertex angles or defect correlation refutes it.
approaches.failure_signature: Model statistics insensitive to line tension versus pure packing at realistic N, so no observable can separate them; or approach 1 data unavailable.

references.note: Weaire and Rivier 1984, Soap, cells and statistics
Politi et al. 2004, Sea urchin spine calcite forms via a transient amorphous calcium carbonate phase

approaches.missing: Depends on approach 1's measured shells for the comparison step; the simulation alone is tractable.

approaches.title: In silico trial: aligned versus uniform lattices with simulated print scatter
approaches.method: Run the experiment computationally with the variability the physical test would face. For each of three load cases (block compression, three-point bending, a 2D femoral-head-like section under hip load), compute principal stress trajectories in the solid design domain (FEniCSx), build a stress-aligned lattice by tracing isostatic lines (Daynes et al. 2017 style) and a uniform lattice (square or triangular) with equal strut count and equal total strut volume. Analyse both as geometrically nonlinear beam frames with an elastic-plastic resin law taken from a stated tough-SLA datasheet, with strut buckling and strut fracture at a stated strain. Emulate print variability by Monte Carlo: strut diameter lognormal with CV 5-10%, node offset noise, and 0-2% missing struts. Outputs per replicate: peak load and energy to a stated failure point (first 20% load drop). Pre-registered pass: aligned mean exceeds uniform mean by more than twice the pooled replicate SD in at least two of three load cases, and the ranking does not reverse in the third.
steps: Pre-register load cases, lattice generation rules, material law, failure definition, variability model and pass criterion.
Implement isostatic-line tracing and equal-mass, equal-strut-count matching.
Run 200 Monte Carlo replicates per design and load case.
Report effect sizes, the variability needed to erase the gain, and sensitivity to the material law.
Export the designs as STL for approach 2.
approaches.decisive_result: Per load case, the standardized gain (aligned minus uniform, over replicate SD) with CIs, and the print-variability CV at which the gain falls below 2 SD.
approaches.failure_signature: Gains that disappear when the strut-count constraint is enforced (alignment advantage was a strut-density artefact), or results dominated by the assumed failure law.

references.note: Daynes, Feih, Lu and Wei 2017, Optimisation of functionally graded lattice structures using isostatic lines
Tam and Mueller 2017, Additive manufacturing along principal stress lines
Sigmund, Aage and Andreassen 2016, On the (non-)optimality of Michell structures
Deshpande, Ashby and Fleck 2001, Foam topology: bending versus stretching dominated architectures

approaches.missing: A simulation is not the printed test the problem asks for; it predicts the effect and the variability that would erase it.

approaches.title: Operator-ready pre-registration and design package for the printed test
approaches.method: The swarm cannot print or test, but it can make the physical experiment cheap for an operator or a collaborator found on the Science Claw forum. Deliver: STL files for aligned and uniform lattices for three load cases (from approach 1), mass and strut count verified from the meshes, a fixture drawing, a print protocol (orientation, layer height, post-cure), a test protocol (crosshead speed, failure definition), and a power analysis. With n = 10 replicates per arm, two-sided alpha 0.05 and 80% power, a two-sample t-test detects a standardized effect of about d = 1.32; the in silico effect from approach 1 says whether n = 10 is enough or more replicates are needed. Mass of each printed specimen is weighed and used as a covariate. Post the package with claim ids thompson1917-ch16-05 and -06 to the forum and log results through delphi_log_test_result when returned.
steps: Generate and check STL files (watertight, minimum strut diameter above printer resolution).
Write the pre-registration with hypotheses, analysis (ANCOVA on peak load with mass covariate; Holm correction across load cases) and stopping rules.
Post a call for an operator on the forum; register the pre-registration before any printing.
When data return, run the pre-registered analysis unchanged.
approaches.decisive_result: Peak load and energy to failure for at least 10 printed replicates per arm per load case, analysed as pre-registered.
approaches.failure_signature: No operator prints the specimens within the month, or print-to-print mass variation exceeds 5% so equal-mass matching fails.

references.note: Wu, Aage, Westermann and Sigmund 2018, Infill optimization for additive manufacturing: approaching bone-like porous structures
Aage et al. 2017, Giga-voxel computational morphogenesis for structural design

approaches.missing: An SLA printer, tough resin, a universal testing machine and an operator; the swarm can only prepare the design and analysis.

approaches.title: Meta-analysis of published aligned-versus-uniform lattice tests at matched mass
approaches.method: Many additive-manufacturing papers compare stress-aligned, isostatic-line or functionally graded lattices with uniform ones experimentally. Extract all such physical comparisons (any printing process, reported separately for SLA) with matched mass or relative density, recording whether strut count was also matched. The effect size is the log ratio of peak load (and of energy absorption where reported) with its SE from replicate data. Fit a random-effects model with moderators: process, load case type, strut-count matching, stiffness contrast. The problem's question about whether gains survive process variability is addressed by comparing the pooled effect to the within-study replicate CV.
steps: Pre-register search strings (Europe PMC, Crossref), inclusion criteria (physical tests, matched mass within 5%, at least 3 replicates per arm) and the model.
Screen and extract with provenance; two agents per paper.
Fit the random-effects model, report pooled log ratio with CI, I^2 and funnel asymmetry.
Report the subset matched on both mass and strut count separately, since it is the one the problem specifies.
approaches.decisive_result: Pooled log peak-load ratio with 95% CI from at least eight independent physical comparisons, and the estimate in the mass-and-strut-count-matched subset.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than eight eligible studies, or none matched on strut count, so the problem's exact comparison cannot be estimated; strong funnel asymmetry.

references.note: Daynes, Feih, Lu and Wei 2017, Optimisation of functionally graded lattice structures using isostatic lines
Tam and Mueller 2017, Additive manufacturing along principal stress lines

approaches.missing: Published comparisons rarely match strut count and often report single specimens; publication bias toward positive gains is likely.
